sections.title: Customer Identification and Segmentation
sections.summary: Quality management begins with understanding who the customer is. Organizations serve multiple customer types — external end users, internal process customers, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders. Segmentation allows organizations to tailor quality strategies to different customer groups with different needs, expectations, and value drivers.

concepts.definition: External customers: end users who purchase or use the product/service. Internal customers: downstream processes or departments that receive the output of an upstream process. Intermediate customers: distributors, retailers, or partners who deliver the product to end users. Regulatory/statutory customers: government agencies enforcing compliance requirements. Each type has distinct quality requirements that the QMS must address.
concepts.examTip: Internal customer concept is frequently tested — every process has a customer (the next process). Treating internal handoffs as customer-supplier relationships improves overall quality.

concepts.definition: Dividing the customer base into distinct groups that share common characteristics, needs, or behaviors. Segmentation bases: demographic (age, income, industry, company size), geographic (region, climate, urban/rural), behavioral (usage rate, loyalty, purchase occasion), psychographic (values, lifestyle), needs-based (functional requirements, service expectations). Quality strategies should be differentiated by segment.
concepts.examTip: Not all customers are equal in value or requirements. Segmentation enables resource allocation — premium segments may justify higher quality investment.

concepts.definition: Identify all interested parties and their quality-related requirements: customers (product performance), employees (safe work environment), shareholders (financial returns), regulators (compliance), community (environmental impact), suppliers (clear specifications, fair terms). ISO 9001:2015 Clause 4.2 explicitly requires understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties.
concepts.examTip: Interested parties ≠ just customers. ISO 9001:2015 broadened scope to all relevant interested parties — know the distinction.

practiceQuestions.q: A quality manager argues that the manufacturing department's only customer is the end user who purchases the product. This view is INCOMPLETE because:
options: End users are not the most important customer
It ignores internal customers — downstream processes that receive manufacturing output
Regulatory agencies are the primary customer
practiceQuestions.explanation: Every process has an internal customer — the next process in the value chain. Manufacturing's immediate customers include assembly, test, and packaging departments. Ignoring internal customer requirements causes defects that propagate to the end user.

flashcards.back: Internal: next process in the value chain within the organization. External: entity outside the organization who receives the final product/service. Both have requirements that must be identified, communicated, and met. Juran emphasized that quality improvement requires treating internal handoffs with the same rigor as external deliveries.

Clause 4.2 requires identifying interested parties relevant to the QMS and their requirements. Beyond customers: employees, owners, suppliers, regulators, society. The organization decides which are relevant and which requirements to address.

sections.title: Voice of the Customer (VOC)
sections.summary: Voice of the Customer is the systematic process of capturing, analyzing, and translating customer needs and expectations into actionable quality requirements. VOC data drives product development, process improvement, and strategic decisions. Quality managers must know the methods, their strengths and limitations, and how to translate qualitative customer language into measurable specifications.

concepts.definition: Reactive methods (customer-initiated): complaints, warranty claims, returns, call center data, social media feedback. Proactive methods (organization-initiated): surveys (structured questionnaires), interviews (in-depth qualitative), focus groups (moderated group discussion), observation/ethnography (watch customers use the product), customer advisory boards (ongoing dialogue with key accounts). Proactive methods are more valuable because they capture unexpressed needs and opportunities.
concepts.examTip: Complaints represent only 4–8% of dissatisfied customers — reactive data dramatically underestimates quality issues. Proactive VOC is essential.

concepts.definition: Classifies customer requirements into categories based on their relationship to satisfaction: Must-Be (basic expectations — absence causes strong dissatisfaction, presence does not increase satisfaction), One-Dimensional (performance — satisfaction increases linearly with fulfillment), Attractive (delighters — unexpected features that create excitement, absence causes no dissatisfaction), Indifferent (customer does not care either way), Reverse (presence causes dissatisfaction for some customers).
concepts.examTip: Must-Be requirements are non-negotiable — failing these causes immediate customer defection regardless of other performance. Attractive requirements differentiate but are temporary — they become Must-Be over time as competitors copy them.

concepts.definition: Structured methodology for translating VOC into technical requirements at every development stage. The House of Quality matrix maps: Customer Requirements (WHATs — left wall), Technical Requirements (HOWs — ceiling), Relationship Matrix (body — strength of linkage between WHATs and HOWs), Correlation Matrix (roof — interactions among HOWs), Competitive Assessment (right wall — benchmarking), Technical Targets (basement — measurable specifications).
concepts.examTip: QFD ensures customer voice is not lost during translation to engineering specifications. The exam tests whether you understand the matrix components and their purpose.

concepts.definition: Decomposes broad customer needs into specific, measurable quality characteristics. Structure: Customer Need (general, qualitative) → Driver (specific aspect of the need) → CTQ (measurable requirement with specification and tolerance). Example: 'Fast delivery' → 'Order processing time' → 'Processing time ≤ 24 hours from order receipt, target 4 hours.'
concepts.examTip: CTQ trees bridge the gap between 'what the customer says' and 'what we measure.' The exam tests whether a CTQ is truly measurable and actionable.

practiceQuestions.q: A hotel chain discovers that clean rooms receive no positive feedback in surveys but immediately generates complaints when standards slip. Using the Kano model, room cleanliness is classified as:
options: Attractive quality — it delights when present
Must-be quality — expected baseline, no upside from exceeding
Indifferent quality — customers do not notice either way
practiceQuestions.explanation: Room cleanliness is a Must-Be requirement: its presence is simply expected (no satisfaction increase), but its absence causes immediate, strong dissatisfaction. Must-Be requirements must be met consistently but do not create competitive advantage.

practiceQuestions.q: In a QFD House of Quality, the 'roof' (correlation matrix) identifies:
options: Links between customer requirements and technical requirements
practiceQuestions.explanation: The roof of the House of Quality shows correlations (positive and negative) among technical requirements. This reveals trade-offs — improving one technical parameter may worsen another — which is critical for design optimization.

flashcards.back: Attractive → One-Dimensional → Must-Be. Today's delighters become tomorrow's expectations. Example: GPS navigation in cars was once a luxury feature (Attractive), became a competitive differentiator (One-Dimensional), and is now a basic expectation (Must-Be).

Left wall: Customer requirements (WHATs). Ceiling: Technical requirements (HOWs). Body: Relationship matrix (linkage strength). Roof: Correlation matrix (HOW-to-HOW interactions). Right wall: Competitive assessment. Basement: Technical targets and benchmarks.

Reactive: complaints, returns, warranty — captures failures. Proactive: surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation — captures needs, expectations, and opportunities. Best practice: use both. Proactive methods capture the 90%+ of dissatisfied customers who never complain.

Single-question metric: 'How likely are you to recommend us?' (0–10 scale). Promoters (9–10) − Detractors (0–6) = NPS. Passives (7–8) excluded. World-class: NPS > 50. Strength: simplicity. Weakness: one number cannot diagnose root causes of satisfaction or dissatisfaction.

sections.title: Customer Satisfaction and Loyalty
sections.summary: Measuring and improving customer satisfaction is a fundamental quality management responsibility. This section covers satisfaction measurement methods, the economics of customer retention, complaint management systems, and the relationship between service quality, satisfaction, and loyalty. The exam tests both measurement methodology and strategic application.

concepts.definition: Methods range from transactional surveys (after specific interactions) to relationship surveys (periodic assessment of overall satisfaction). Key design principles: measure what matters to the customer (not what is easy to measure), use consistent scales, benchmark against competitors, track trends over time, close the loop (act on feedback). Common metrics: CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score), NPS (Net Promoter Score), CES (Customer Effort Score).
concepts.formula:
CSAT = (Satisfied responses / Total responses) × 100%
NPS = % Promoters (9-10) − % Detractors (0-6)
CES = Average of effort ratings (typically 1-7 scale)
concepts.examTip: CSAT measures satisfaction with a specific transaction. NPS measures likelihood to recommend (loyalty proxy). CES measures ease of interaction. Each answers a different question — use the right metric for the right purpose.

concepts.definition: Measures service quality through five dimensions: Tangibles (physical facilities, equipment, staff appearance), Reliability (ability to perform the promised service dependably), Responsiveness (willingness to help, promptness), Assurance (knowledge, courtesy, ability to inspire trust), Empathy (caring, individualized attention). Quality = Perception − Expectation across all five dimensions.
concepts.formula:
Service Quality Gap = Perception Score − Expectation Score
Negative gap = quality shortfall
Positive gap = quality exceeds expectations
concepts.examTip: Remember the five dimensions with the acronym 'RATER' (Reliability, Assurance, Tangibles, Empathy, Responsiveness). Reliability is consistently rated as the most important dimension across industries.

concepts.definition: Acquiring a new customer costs 5–7 times more than retaining an existing one. A 5% increase in retention can increase profits by 25–95% (Reichheld). Loyal customers: buy more frequently, try new products, refer others, are less price-sensitive, cost less to serve. Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) quantifies the total revenue a customer generates over the entire relationship.
concepts.formula:
CLV = (Average Annual Revenue × Gross Margin %) × Avg. Customer Lifespan − Acquisition Cost
Simplified CLV = Annual Profit per Customer / Annual Churn Rate
concepts.examTip: CLV arguments are powerful for justifying quality investments — frame quality improvements in terms of customer retention impact.

concepts.definition: Systematic process for handling customer complaints: Receive and acknowledge promptly, Log and categorize, Investigate root cause, Resolve and communicate resolution to customer, Follow up to verify satisfaction, Analyze aggregate complaint data for systemic improvement. A well-managed complaint can increase loyalty (the 'service recovery paradox' — customers whose complaints are handled well may become more loyal than those who never experienced a problem).
concepts.examTip: Complaints are a gift — they provide free VOC data. The key metric is resolution time and first-contact resolution rate, not just complaint volume.

practiceQuestions.q: A SERVQUAL analysis shows the largest gap (Perception − Expectation) is in the Reliability dimension. This means:
options: Customers perceive the physical facilities as inadequate
Customers feel employees lack knowledge and courtesy
The organization is failing to deliver its promised service dependably
Customers want more personalized, empathetic attention
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reliability is 'the ability to perform the promised service dependably and accurately.' A gap in this dimension means customers perceive the organization as not delivering on its commitments — the most damaging service quality failure.

practiceQuestions.q: Customer data shows: annual revenue per customer = $10,000, gross margin = 40%, average lifespan = 5 years, acquisition cost = $2,000. The CLV is:

flashcards.back: Reliability: deliver as promised. Assurance: knowledge and courtesy inspiring trust. Tangibles: physical evidence of service. Empathy: caring, individualized attention. Responsiveness: willingness to help promptly. Reliability ranks #1 in importance across most industries.

A customer whose complaint is resolved exceptionally well may become more loyal than a customer who never had a problem. Conditions: the failure was perceived as not severe, recovery was swift and exceeded expectations, and the failure was seen as an isolated incident.

Measures how easy it was for the customer to get their issue resolved. Research suggests CES is a better predictor of repurchase behavior than CSAT or NPS. Principle: reducing customer effort drives loyalty more than delighting customers.
